Sample Size Planning for a Single Regression Coefficient (AIPE)

Source: R/ss_aipe_reg_coef.R
ss_aipe_reg_coef.Rd

Computes the necessary sample size for the confidence interval on a targeted regression coefficient \(\beta_j\), the quantity true_reg_coef_j stands for, in a multiple regression with p predictors to be no wider than a user-specified value. The coefficient is on the scale true_sd_Y and true_sd_X describe: with both 1, the default, its population value is the standardized coefficient. This is the accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) framework of Kelley and Maxwell (2003), targeted at a specific coefficient rather than at the omnibus \(R^2\). The default (noncentral = FALSE) plans for the central t interval for the coefficient in the units of the data, the interval ci_rc reports; noncentral = TRUE plans for the noncentral t interval for the standardized coefficient (Kelley, 2007a), the interval ci_src reports, with unit standard deviations. The central t interval for the standardized coefficient, the interval of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 1), is a third interval, and ss_aipe_src with noncentral = FALSE plans for it; see "The interval planned for" in Details. Supplying assurance returns the smallest N, not below the plan without it (the plan for the width at the expected values of the sample squared multiple correlations), at which the realized interval is no wider than width with at least that probability, computed exactly for the central interval; for the noncentral interval it returns by default the published approximation that MBESS uses, which does not compute the probability, and with assurance_method = "simulation" the smallest N at which a simulated estimate of the probability reaches the request.

Usage

ss_aipe_reg_coef(
  true_R2_Y_X = NULL,
  true_R2_j_X_without_j = NULL,
  p = NULL,
  true_reg_coef_j = NULL,
  width,
  which_width = "Full",
  true_sd_Y = 1,
  true_sd_X = 1,
  true_cor_XX = NULL,
  true_cor_YX = NULL,
  which_predictor = NULL,
  noncentral = FALSE,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  assurance = NULL,
  assurance_method = c("analytic", "simulation"),
  G = 20000,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

true_R2_Y_X

Population value of \(\rho^2_{Y \cdot X_1, \ldots, X_p}\), the squared multiple correlation of the outcome Y with all p predictors.

true_R2_j_X_without_j

Population value of \(\rho^2_{X_j \cdot X_{-j}}\), the squared multiple correlation when the jth predictor is regressed on the remaining \(p - 1\) predictors. Quantifies the multicollinearity faced by the targeted coefficient.

p

The number of predictor variables.

true_reg_coef_j

Population value \(\beta_j\) of the regression coefficient for the jth predictor, the predictor of interest, on the scale true_sd_Y and true_sd_X describe: with both 1 it is the standardized coefficient, and otherwise the unstandardized one, the standardized coefficient times true_sd_Y / true_sd_X (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, p. 316); \(b_j\) is its sample estimate. On the covariance structure path it may be left out; when it is given it must equal the coefficient the correlations imply on that scale.

width

Desired (full) width of the two-sided confidence interval on \(\beta_j\).

which_width

Which portion of the confidence interval width refers to. Only "Full" (or an abbreviation of it, such as "F") is currently implemented; "Lower", "Upper", and their abbreviations are refused.

true_sd_Y

Population standard deviation of Y, which with true_sd_X sets the scale of the coefficient and of width.

true_sd_X

Population standard deviation of the jth predictor.

true_cor_XX

Population correlation matrix for the p predictor variables. If supplied with true_cor_YX, true_R2_Y_X and true_R2_j_X_without_j are derived from the covariance structure. With one predictor it is matrix(1) (or the number 1), and p and which_predictor are then 1 when not given.

true_cor_YX

Length-p vector of population correlations between Y and the p predictors.

which_predictor

Which of the p predictors is the targeted coefficient.

noncentral

If TRUE, plans for the noncentral t interval for the standardized coefficient (Kelley, 2007a), the interval of ci_src. If FALSE (the default), plans for the central t interval for the coefficient in the units of the data, the interval of ci_rc, even when both standard deviations are 1; the central interval for the standardized coefficient is planned by ss_aipe_src with noncentral = FALSE. The noncentral path requires true_sd_Y = true_sd_X = 1 (i.e., a standardized solution).

alpha_lower

Type I error rate for the lower confidence limit, at least 1e-9 and at most .5. A tail area below 1e-9 is refused: the noncentral t limits lose accuracy there, and the central plan keeps the same floor.

alpha_upper

Type I error rate for the upper confidence limit, at least 1e-9 and at most .5.

conf_level

Confidence level (i.e., \(1 - \alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is the Type I error rate). Default 0.95. Mutually exclusive with alpha_lower and alpha_upper. A level above .999999998, whose tail areas are below 1e-9, is refused.

assurance

Optional probability with which the realized confidence interval is to be no wider than width, a single number above .5 and below 1. When NULL (the default), the plan is the smallest N at which the interval is no wider than width when the two sample squared multiple correlations take their expected values (see "The interval planned for" in Details): the width at those expected values, not the mean of the width over samples.

assurance_method

How the probability that the realized interval is no wider than width is found, used only with assurance (see "The assurance step" in Details). "analytic" (the default) computes without simulation: for the central interval (noncentral = FALSE) the probability is exact, and the function returns the smallest sample size, at or above the plan without assurance, at which it is at least assurance, reported as assurance_attained; for the noncentral interval it returns the published approximation that MBESS uses, which does not compute the probability (assurance_attained is NA) and can attain less than assurance. "simulation", offered for the noncentral interval only, returns the smallest sample size, at or above the plan without assurance, at which the probability estimated from G simulated samples is at least assurance, and reports that estimate. With noncentral = FALSE "simulation" is refused with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid, since a simulated estimate of an exact probability would only add Monte Carlo error.

G

Number of simulated samples at each sample size the noncentral assurance step tries, and in its final estimate of the attained probability; a whole number of at least 100 (default 20000). Used and checked only with noncentral = TRUE, assurance, and assurance_method = "simulation".

seed

Optional single number. When given, the noncentral assurance step is reproducible, and the random number stream of the calling session is left as it was. With NULL (the default) the draws come from the session's current stream. Used only where G is.

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value:

necessary_N

the necessary total sample size.

assurance

the requested probability; present only when assurance was given.

assurance_attained

the probability, at necessary_N, that the realized interval is no wider than width; present only when assurance was given. Exact for the central interval; for the noncentral interval NA with assurance_method = "analytic", whose approximation does not compute it, and with "simulation" a Monte Carlo estimate, whose standard error is the attribute assurance_mc_se.

G

the number of simulated samples; present only when the noncentral assurance step simulated.

With assurance the printed footer names the assurance method and says how assurance_attained was found, or that the approximation does not compute it; the attributes assurance_method ("analytic" or "simulation") and assurance_probability ("exact", "simulation", or "not computed") record the same.

Details

Calling conventions. The function offers several mutually exclusive ways to supply the population information needed to plan \(N\); the user picks the one most aligned with their available planning values. Specify exactly one of:

  • Covariance structure path. Supply true_cor_XX and true_cor_YX along with which_predictor. The function derives \(\rho^2_{Y \cdot X}\) and \(\rho^2_{X_j \cdot X_{-j}}\) (the values of true_R2_Y_X and true_R2_j_X_without_j) from the covariance structure, and the population coefficient \(\beta_j\), the jth element of \(R_{XX}^{-1} r_{XY}\) (\(R_{XX}\) is true_cor_XX and \(r_{XY}\) is true_cor_YX) times true_sd_Y / true_sd_X, against which a supplied true_reg_coef_j is checked.

  • Squared multiple correlations path. Supply true_R2_Y_X, true_R2_j_X_without_j, p, and true_reg_coef_j directly when the user already has these planning values from prior research and does not need to specify the full covariance structure.

  • Standardized solution. For the noncentral = TRUE path, set true_sd_Y = true_sd_X = 1; the result returns the standardized regression coefficient sample size.

The interval planned for. With noncentral = FALSE the interval is the central t interval for the coefficient in the units of the data, \(b_j\) plus the t quantiles (on \(N - p - 1\) degrees of freedom) at alpha_lower and 1 - alpha_upper times its standard error, the interval ci_rc and ci_reg_coef report from unstandardized data, and this is so whatever true_sd_Y and true_sd_X are: with both 1 the coefficient is on the standardized scale, but the interval planned for is still the one computed in the units of the data, whose standard error comes from the residual sums of squares of Y and of \(X_j\). The plan without assurance is the smallest N at which that interval, computed at the expected values of the two sample squared multiple correlations, is no wider than width (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, Equations 1 and 2, with the t quantile); the two tails exchanged give the same plan. The plan is the smallest such N of at least \(p + 2\), the smallest sample with a residual degree of freedom, and the expected squared multiple correlation of \(X_j\) with the other predictors is that of a regression on those \(p - 1\) predictors (0 with one predictor; see "Comparison with MBESS"). Kelley and Maxwell's Equation 1 is the central interval for the standardized coefficient, whose standard error is formed from the two sample squared multiple correlations; its plan without assurance is this one at unit standard deviations, but the probability that it is no wider than width is not the probability the assurance step below computes, and ss_aipe_src with noncentral = FALSE plans its assurance. With noncentral = TRUE the interval is the noncentral t interval for the standardized coefficient of ci_src: the limits of the noncentrality parameter at the observed t statistic, times the standard error \(\sqrt{(1 - R^2)/[(1 - R^2_{X_j \cdot X_{-j}})(N - p - 1)]}\), and the plan without assurance is the smallest N, of at least \(p + 2\), at which it is no wider than width at the expected squared multiple correlations and \(\beta_j\). That standard error treats the sample standard deviations as constants, which for random predictors is an approximation (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, pp. 315–316). The central path is fast and adequate at moderate to large N; the noncentral path is the one to use when the analysis will report the noncentral interval for the standardized coefficient. A tail of 0, or two of .5, is refused, and so is a tail area below 1e-9 or a conf_level above .999999998.

The assurance step. A plan without assurance makes the interval as narrow as the target when the sample values equal their expectations; in roughly half of all samples it is wider. With assurance the function plans so that the realized interval is no wider than width with at least that probability, for random predictors from a multivariate normal population.

  • The central interval (noncentral = FALSE). The only method is "analytic": the function computes \(P_N\), the probability that the realized interval is no wider than width at sample size N, exactly, and returns the smallest N, at or above the plan without assurance, at which \(P_N\) is at least assurance, found by doubling a step upward and then bisecting. assurance_attained is \(P_N\) at the returned N. The squared standard error of \(b_j\) is the residual sum of squares of Y on all p predictors over \(N - p - 1\), divided by the residual sum of squares of \(X_j\) on the other \(p - 1\). Under multivariate normality the first, over \(\sigma^2_Y (1 - \rho^2_{Y \cdot X})\), is chi square on \(N - p - 1\) degrees of freedom whatever the predictors are, so it is independent of the second, which over \(\sigma^2_{X_j} (1 - \rho^2_{X_j \cdot X_{-j}})\) is chi square on \(N - p\) degrees of freedom. The squared standard error is then \(K F / (N - p)\), with \(K = \sigma^2_Y (1 - \rho^2_{Y \cdot X}) / [\sigma^2_{X_j} (1 - \rho^2_{X_j \cdot X_{-j}})]\) and F an F variate on \(N - p - 1\) and \(N - p\) degrees of freedom, and with \(q\) the sum of the two t quantiles of the interval, $$P_N = \Pr(F \le w^2 (N - p) / (q^2 K)),$$ where \(w\) is width. (With fixed predictors the second sum of squares is a constant and the same event is a chi square probability; the plan is for random predictors, the model ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity simulates.) The units of Y and \(X_j\) cancel, so changing them, with width changed to match, leaves the plan as it was, and the sign of \(\beta_j\) does not enter.

  • The noncentral interval (noncentral = TRUE). The width depends on the observed t statistic and on both sample squared multiple correlations, and no closed form for its distribution is used. With assurance_method = "analytic", the default, the plan is the approximation that MBESS uses (Kelley, 2007a, 2007b): the plan without assurance made again with a lower confidence limit (at level assurance) of the squared multiple correlation in place of its population value, and not below the first. It does not compute the probability it attains, so assurance_attained is NA, and the printed footer says so. Kelley and Maxwell (2008, pp. 186–187) wrote that no satisfactory method then existed for the standardized coefficient and described finding, by simulation, the smallest sample size that attains the requested degree of certainty, which is what assurance_method = "simulation" does: \(P_N\) is estimated as the proportion of G samples, drawn from the exact sampling distribution of the sums of squares and products (Wishart, through the entries of its triangular factor that the statistics depend on), whose interval is no wider than width. The same G samples serve every sample size the search tries (common random numbers: each chi square entry is the quantile, at the degrees of freedom of that N, of one uniform draw), so the estimate changes smoothly with N. The search assumes that it does not decrease as N grows, which held in every set checked although a single simulated interval can be wider at \(N + 1\) than at N (see below), and under that assumption the step returns the smallest N at which the estimate is at least assurance. The distribution of the width depends on the population through p, \(\beta_j\), the two squared multiple correlations, and the correlation of Y with \(X_j\). On the covariance structure path that correlation is given; on the squared multiple correlations path it is not, and the step uses the smallest estimated probability over 21 equally spaced values of it, from the smallest to the largest that the three values allow. That is an approximate minimum over the range: between two of the values the probability can be a little lower than at either, so for a correlation there the plan can fall a little short of the request. (With \(p = 2\) only the two ends of the range are possible, and the step uses both.) assurance_attained is the estimate at the returned N, so it is at least assurance, and its Monte Carlo standard error is the attribute assurance_mc_se. The exact \(P_N\) differs from the estimate by that error, so the returned N can be a case or two from the one the exact probability would give, and \(P_N\) there can be a little below assurance; give seed for a plan that can be reproduced, and a larger G for a more precise one. Reversing the sign of \(\beta_j\) (with alpha_lower and alpha_upper exchanged when they differ) gives the same plan.

For both intervals \(P_N\) did not decrease from one N to the next at or above the plan without assurance: for the central interval in 1,530 planning sets (p from 1 to 15, squared multiple correlations from 0 to .9, widths from .05 to 2, and tails of .025 and .025, .005 and .005, and .01 and .04) over every N from that plan to three times it, and for the noncentral interval in five sets by simulation. With the samples held fixed across N, the estimate did not decrease from one N to the next in seven sets (p from 1 to 10), and of 95 million comparisons of a simulated interval at N and at \(N + 1\), 3208, all at N below 60, were wider at \(N + 1\). Below the plan without assurance \(P_N\) can decrease, which is why the search starts there.

The approximations can attain more or less than the request. For two predictors correlated .3 with correlations of .4 and .3 with Y, a width of .3, and an assurance of .90, the chi square approximation of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3; 2008, Equation 37) for the central interval, the plan without assurance with the variance of \(b_j\) multiplied by the assurance quantile of a chi square on \(N - 1\) degrees of freedom over \(N - p - 1\), is 181, at which \(P_N\) is .852, and the exact plan is 187 (\(P_N\) = .902); the noncentral approximation, the default plan for that interval, is 179, at which the simulated probability is .948, and assurance_method = "simulation" returns 176 (.908 with seed = 1). For the five exchangeable predictors of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, pp. 312–313), correlated .4 with one another and .3 with Y, at a width of .2 and an assurance of .80, the chi square approximation is 486 (\(P_N\) = .765) and the exact plan 491 (.800). Each was checked against the proportion of intervals no wider than the target among samples of raw multivariate normal data. These probabilities, and those of the first example, are for the central interval in the units of the data, the interval this function plans for. Kelley and Maxwell's example is of the standardized coefficient, with the central interval for it (their Equation 1), which is computed from standardized data with the sample standard deviations treated as constants; its width varies less, and it is no wider than .2 with probability .877 at 486 and .911 at 491 (their own simulation, p. 317, reported .816 at their plan of 485, where raw multivariate normal data give .871 with the t quantile of their Equation 1, or .887 with the normal quantile of their plan). For that interval ss_aipe_src with noncentral = FALSE, assurance_method = "simulation", and seed = 1 plans 478 (.807, and .797 at 477), and in the first example 171 (.914, and .895 at 170), where the plans above reach .986 at 181 and .997 at 187; its plan is simulated, and another seed can give one a case away (170 for one of seeds 1 to 30 in the first example).

Comparison with MBESS. The plans without assurance of ss.aipe.reg.coef() in MBESS differ from these in two ways. They take the expected squared multiple correlation of \(X_j\) with the other predictors to be that of a regression on p predictors, where that regression has \(p - 1\), which overstates it and so the width. And their search goes up one case at a time from a start, the larger of \(2p + 1\) and ten below the normal approximation for the central interval and six below the central plan for the noncentral one, so it returns the start when a smaller sample size already meets the width: for true_R2_Y_X = .8, true_R2_j_X_without_j = 0, p = 10, and width = 2, 21 where 14 does. In 1,530 planning sets the two differences make the central plan here one case smaller in 1,329 and 2 to 13 cases smaller in 104, and in 810 sets the noncentral plan one smaller in 596 and 2 to 10 smaller in 177. The approximations start from these plans (Kelley and Maxwell's example above is 487 in MBESS and 486 here). With unequal tails ss.aipe.reg.coef() also takes both t quantiles of its central plans at the average of the two tails, so it plans for an interval narrower than the one ci_rc reports; the central plans here take the quantile at each tail.

References

Kelley, K. (2007a). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K. (2007b). Methods for the behavioral, educational, and social sciences: An R package. Behavior Research Methods, 39(4), 979–984. doi:10.3758/BF03192993

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2008). Sample size planning with applications to multiple regression: Power and accuracy for omnibus and targeted effects. In P. Alasuutari, L. Bickman, & J. Brannen (Eds.), The Sage handbook of social research methods (pp. 166–192). Sage.

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 4 on individual comparisons of means and Chapter 6 on trend analysis.)

Maxwell, S. E., Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2008). Sample size planning for statistical power and accuracy in parameter estimation. Annual Review of Psychology, 59, 537–563. doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.59.103006.093735

See also

ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity, ci_nc_t

design_consequences for what a chosen design delivers: power, the Type S (sign) and Type M (exaggeration) errors of the significance filter, and the expected confidence interval width.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# 1. Covariance structure path: supply the population correlation
#    matrix and the population YX cross-correlations. Five predictors
#    in an exchangeable structure (all pairwise correlations 0.5,
#    all Y-X correlations 0.3).
true_cor_YX <- c(.3, .3, .3, .3, .3)
true_cor_XX <- rbind(c(1, .5, .5, .5, .5), c(.5, 1, .5, .5, .5),
                c(.5, .5, 1, .5, .5), c(.5, .5, .5, 1, .5),
                c(.5, .5, .5, .5, 1))

# Closed-form (central t) planning, targeting the first predictor's
# standardized coefficient.
ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .10, which_width = "Full",
                 true_sd_Y = 1, true_sd_X = 1,
                 true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,
                 which_predictor = 1, noncentral = FALSE,
                 conf_level = .95)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 2184 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# With an assurance of .85: the smallest N at which the realized
# interval is no wider than 0.10 with probability at least .85. The
# last row is that probability at the returned N, computed exactly.
ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .10, which_width = "Full",
                 true_sd_Y = 1, true_sd_X = 1,
                 true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,
                 which_predictor = 1, noncentral = FALSE,
                 conf_level = .95, assurance = .85)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        2281 
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained 0.850
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Assurance method: analytic; assurance_attained is the exact probability that the interval is no wider than the width

# The noncentral t interval for the standardized coefficient. Required
# N differs at small to moderate samples.
ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .10, which_width = "Full",
                 true_sd_Y = 1, true_sd_X = 1,
                 true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,
                 which_predictor = 1, noncentral = TRUE,
                 conf_level = .95)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 2190 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# With assurance its default plan is the approximation that MBESS uses,
# which does not compute the probability it attains; by simulation, the
# smallest N at which the estimated probability is at least .85. G = 2000
# keeps the example quick; a reported plan deserves the default G = 20000.
ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .10, true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX,
                 true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX, which_predictor = 1,
                 noncentral = TRUE, assurance = .85)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        2240 
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained <NA> 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Assurance method: analytic; the plan is the published approximation, which does not compute the probability that the interval is no wider than the width (assurance_attained is NA) and can attain less than the assurance. assurance_method = "simulation" computes it and returns the smallest plan that attains it
plan <- ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .10, true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX,
                         true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX, which_predictor = 1,
                         noncentral = TRUE, assurance = .85,
                         assurance_method = "simulation",
                         G = 2000, seed = 113)
plan
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        2257 
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained 0.854
#>  G                  2000 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Assurance method: simulation; assurance_attained is estimated from G = 2000 simulated samples (Monte Carlo SE 0.008)
attr(plan, "assurance_mc_se")
#> [1] 0.007895695

# 2. Squared multiple correlations path: when the user has planning
#    values for true_R2_Y_X and true_R2_j_X_without_j directly (e.g.,
#    from a prior power analysis), without specifying the full
#    covariance structure. true_reg_coef_j is required on this path.
ss_aipe_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = 0.30, true_R2_j_X_without_j = 0.20,
                 p = 5, true_reg_coef_j = 0.25,
                 width = .15, which_width = "Full",
                 true_sd_Y = 1, true_sd_X = 1,
                 noncentral = FALSE, conf_level = .95)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 606  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 3. One predictor: its correlation matrix is matrix(1), and p and
#    which_predictor follow from it.
ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .20, true_cor_XX = matrix(1), true_cor_YX = .4)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 327  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
